title: IoT Protocols Part 1: OSI, TCP/IP, IoT Protocol Stack, CoAP, MQTT, XMPP, DDS, AMQP — Exam Revision
description: Exam revision of IoT protocols, part 1: the OSI model, the TCP/IP suite, the IoT protocol stack (link, network, transport and application layers), Ethernet, Wi-Fi, WiMax, LR-WPAN, cellular, IPv4, IPv6, 6LoWPAN, TCP vs UDP, HTTP, and the IoT application protocols CoAP, MQTT, XMPP, DDS and AMQP.

scenes.title: What is an IoT protocol?
lines: How do billions of different IoT gadgets actually understand each other?
Through IoT protocols.
IoT protocols enable devices to exchange data in a structured and meaningful way.
They serve as the platform that IoT devices use in order to communicate.
In part one, we cover the network models, every layer of the IoT protocol stack, and the five IoT application protocols.

scenes.title: The OSI model
lines: First, the Network OSI model. It has seven layers.
Application: to allow access to network resources.
Presentation: to translate, encrypt, and compress data.
Session: to establish, manage, and terminate sessions.
Transport: to provide reliable process to process message delivery, and error recovery.
Network: to move packets from source to destination, and to provide internetworking.
Data link: to organize bits into frames, and to provide hop to hop delivery.
Physical: to transmit bits over a medium, and to provide mechanical and electrical specifications.
A memory trick, from the top: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.

scenes.title: The TCP/IP protocol suite
lines: The TCP/IP protocol suite is simpler, with five layers.
The application layer holds several application protocols.
The transport layer holds several transport protocols.
The network layer holds the Internet Protocol, and some helping protocols.
And the data link and physical layers are the underlying LAN and WAN technology.
Notice that application, presentation and session from OSI are merged into one application layer.

scenes.title: The IoT protocol stack
lines: Now the IoT protocol stack. It has four layers.
The Link layer: 802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 Wi-Fi, 802.16 WiMax, 802.15.4 LR-WPAN, and 2G, 3G and 4G cellular.
The Network or Internet layer: IPv4, IPv6, and 6LoWPAN.
The Transport layer: TCP and UDP.
And the Application layer: HTTP, CoAP, WebSocket, MQTT, XMPP, DDS and AMQP.
Learn the full forms.
CoAP is Constrained Application Protocol. XMPP is Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol.
DDS is Data Distribution Service. MQTT is Message Queuing Telemetry Transport.
AMQP is Advanced Message Queuing Protocol. And 6LoWPAN is IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks.

scenes.title: Link layer and 802.3 Ethernet
lines: Layer one: the Link layer.
The link layer determines how the data is physically sent over the network's physical layer.
For example, over copper wire, optical fibre cable, or radio waves.
The first example is 802.3, Ethernet.
It uses coaxial cables, twisted pair wire, or optical fibre as the medium.
Its variants include 802.3 over coaxial cable, 802.3i over copper twisted pair, 802.3j over fibre optics, and 802.3ae over fibre, and so on.
Ethernet data rates range from ten megabits per second up to forty gigabits per second.

scenes.title: 802.11 Wi-Fi
lines: Next, 802.11, Wi-Fi. It is a Wireless LAN.
Common versions are 802.11 b, g and n, in the 2.4 gigahertz and 5 gigahertz bands.
Data rates range from one megabit per second up to 6.75 gigabits per second.
Know the bands of each version.
802.11a operates at 5 gigahertz.
802.11b and g operate at 2.4 gigahertz.
802.11n operates at 2.4 or 5 gigahertz.
802.11ac operates at 5 gigahertz.
And 802.11ad operates at 60 gigahertz.

scenes.title: 802.16 WiMax and 802.15.4 LR-WPAN
lines: 802.16, WiMax, is a collection of wireless broadband standards, with data rates from 1.5 megabits per second to 1 gigabit per second.
802.15.4, LR-WPAN, means Low-Rate Wireless Personal Area Networks. An example given is LoRa.
Its data rate is from forty kilobits to two hundred fifty kilobits per second.
It provides low cost, low speed communication for low power, power constrained devices.
It supports two topologies. In a star, every device talks to one central PAN coordinator.
In peer to peer, devices can talk to each other directly.
The legend shows three node types: the PAN Coordinator, the FFD, or full function device, and the RFD, or reduced function device.

scenes.title: 2G, 3G and 4G mobile communication
lines: The last link layer example is 2G, 3G and 4G mobile communication.
2G uses GSM and CDMA.
3G uses UMTS and CDMA2000.
4G uses LTE.
Data rates range from 9.6 kilobits per second in 2G, up to 100 megabits per second in 4G.

scenes.title: Network layer and IPv4
lines: Layer two: the Network layer.
It is responsible for sending IP datagrams from a source network to the destination network.
It performs host addressing and packet routing.
First, IPv4. It is a thirty two bit address scheme, so a total of two to the power thirty two addresses are available.
An IPv4 address is written in dotted decimal notation, like 172.16.254.1.
Each number is one byte, eight bits. Four bytes make thirty two bits.
IPv4 addresses got exhausted in 2011.
Guaranteed delivery and data integrity are handled by upper layer protocols, for example TCP.
IPv4 is formally described in RFC 791.

scenes.title: IPv6
lines: Next, IPv6. It is a one hundred twenty eight bit address scheme, so two to the power one twenty eight addresses are available.
That is about 3.4 times ten to the power thirty eight addresses.
An IPv6 address is eight groups of four hex digits. Each group goes from zero zero zero zero through F F F F.
The first part is the network prefix, and the last part is the interface ID.
IPv6 is formally described in RFC 2460.

scenes.title: 6LoWPAN
lines: The third network protocol is 6LoWPAN: IPv6 over Low power Wireless Personal Area Networks.
It brings IPv6 to low power devices with limited processing capabilities.
It operates in the 2.4 gigahertz range, with a data transfer rate of 250 kilobits per second.
And it works with the 802.15.4 link layer protocols.

scenes.title: Transport layer and TCP
lines: Layer three: the Transport layer.
Transport layer protocols provide end to end message transfer, independent of the underlying network.
First, TCP: the Transmission Control Protocol.
It is connection oriented, and a stateful protocol.
It ensures reliable transmission, and provides error detection, flow control and congestion control.
It is the most widely used transport layer protocol, and ensures reliable transmission of packets, in order.
It helps avoid network congestion and congestion collapse.
The diagram shows TCP connection states: ESTABLISHED while data flows, then FIN and ACK messages, until the connection is CLOSED.

scenes.title: UDP
lines: Second, UDP: the User Datagram Protocol.
It is a connectionless and stateless protocol.
It is an asynchronous protocol.
It suits time sensitive applications.
It is transaction oriented, and stateless.
And there is no guaranteed delivery. A UDP packet is simply sent.

scenes.title: TCP vs UDP
lines: Compare the two.
TCP gives slower, but reliable transfers.
Typical TCP applications are email and web browsing. TCP is unicast only.
UDP gives fast, but non-guaranteed transfers. This is called best effort.
Typical UDP applications are VoIP, and music streaming.
And UDP supports unicast, multicast, and broadcast.

scenes.title: Application layer and HTTP
lines: Layer four: the Application layer.
An application layer protocol defines how applications interface with the lower layer protocols to send data over a network.
The first example is HTTP, the Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
HTTP is the foundation of the World Wide Web.
It follows a request response model.
It is a stateless protocol.
And it uses URIs, Universal Resource Identifiers, to name resources.

scenes.title: CoAP
lines: CoAP, the Constrained Application Protocol.
It is freely available, and usable for any IoT device.
It is designed to address the needs of HTTP based IoT systems.
CoAP relies on UDP for establishing secure communication between endpoints.
CoAP features Quality of Service, with acknowledgement messages.
It fully addresses the need for an extremely light protocol, for battery operated or low energy devices.
And CoAP is a good match for web service based IoT systems.

scenes.title: MQTT
lines: MQTT, Message Queuing Telemetry Transport.
It is a widely adopted standard in the Industrial Internet of Things, IIoT.
Its architecture is a simple and lightweight publish subscribe, or pub sub, messaging protocol.
It is designed for battery powered devices.
MQTT is based on the publisher, broker and subscriber model. The publisher sends to the broker, and the broker forwards to subscribers.
Its features: minimum bandwidth use, and suited to wireless networks.
Low energy consumption, and good reliability.
And little processing and memory resources.

scenes.title: XMPP
lines: XMPP, Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol.
It was developed by the open source community.
It is an IoT protocol for message oriented middleware, based on the XML language.
It allows real time exchange of structured, but extensible data, between two or more network clients.
Its drawbacks: no Quality of Service,
and no end to end encryption.

scenes.title: DDS
lines: DDS, Data Distribution Service.
It falls under the publish subscribe methodology.
It was designed by the Object Management Group, OMG.
It is for real time M2M communication.
It enables scalable, reliable, high performance and interoperable data exchange between connected devices,
independent of the hardware and the software platform.

scenes.title: Applications of DDS
lines: DDS is used in Industrial Internet of Things deployments, such as
air traffic control, smart grid management, and autonomous vehicles,
transportation systems, robotics, and power generation,
and healthcare services.
Overall, DDS can be used to manage data exchange between lightweight devices, and to interconnect large, high performance sensor networks.

scenes.title: AMQP and its limitation
lines: AMQP, Advanced Message Queuing Protocol.
It is an open standard, publish subscribe type protocol.
It has its roots in the financial services sector.
Its features are message orientation, queuing,
routing, including point to point and publish and subscribe,
and reliability and security.
AMQP can guarantee complete transactions.
Its limitation: due to its heaviness, AMQP is not suitable for sensor devices with limited memory, power, or network bandwidth.

scenes.title: Exam recap
lines: Quick recap.
OSI has seven layers. TCP/IP has five. The IoT stack has four: link, network, transport, application.
Link: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, WiMax, LR-WPAN, cellular. Network: IPv4 thirty two bit, IPv6 one twenty eight bit, 6LoWPAN.
Transport: TCP is reliable and connection oriented. UDP is fast, connectionless, best effort.
CoAP: lightweight, over UDP, for web style IoT. MQTT: lightweight pub sub with a broker, for IIoT.
XMPP: XML based, but no QoS and no encryption. DDS: pub sub by OMG, real time.
AMQP: pub sub from finance, guarantees transactions, but too heavy for sensors.
Good luck in your exam!
